extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers, and policy-interested public
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopedic article summarizing definitions, types, methods, rationales, legal examples, historical cases, effects, and technical implementations of censorship across media and jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship is the suppression of speech, public communication, or other information on the basis that such material is considered objectionable, harmful, sensitive, or 'inconvenient'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be conducted by governments and private institutions; includes self-censorship by creators; occurs across media (speech, books, music, film, press, radio, television, Internet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal of materials that are obscene or otherwise considered morally questionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often targets pornography (especially child pornography) and material deemed to deprave or corrupt; justification and definitions of 'obscene' vary across time and jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping military intelligence and tactics confidential to safeguard national security and maintain public support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to counter espionage and protect operations (examples: WWI/WWII letter censorship, 'Loose lips sink ships'); involves delaying or redacting operational information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship of political opinions in violation of freedoms of speech, press, or assembly, often used to prevent dissent or control public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods include concealing, distorting, falsifying, blacklisting, imprisonment, and assassination; examples include state media control, bans on political parties, and media blackouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting or controlling expression using religious authority or on the basis of religious teachings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically widespread (e.g., Index Librorum Prohibitorum, Galileo affair); also includes contemporary restrictions such as censoring depictions of religious figures to avoid controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervention by corporate media editors or owners to disrupt publishing of information that portrays their business or partners negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can include editorial suppression, selective reporting, and refusal to publish critical pieces; may be driven by business relationships or advertiser pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational censorship / textbook whitewashing
rubrics_metrics.description: Controlling how facts and history are presented in schools, including omissions, edits, or biased framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: edited versions of novels for classrooms, state policies restricting teaching of critical perspectives on race or sexuality; termed 'whitewashing' and often politically contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic-induced censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship enacted indirectly by market forces that commodify or privatize access to information, making it inaccessible to many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes paywalled academic journals, industry reports, and market-driven content suppression; illustrated by instances where economic pressure or regulations remove content from public view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of censoring or classifying one's own discourse out of fear or deference to others' sensibilities or perceived preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common among journalists, publishers, artists, and social media users; surveys show many journalists avoid or tone down stories due to organizational or safety concerns; results from fear of physical/psychological violence or professional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy, picture, and writer approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices giving sources or subjects rights to read/amend articles, choose photos, or select friendly writers, which can function as censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy approval: right to read/amend interviews; picture approval: right to choose photos; writer approval: selecting writers based on expected flattering coverage—can limit critical reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse censorship (information flooding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flooding the public with false or misleading information to distort or drown out disfavored speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practiced by state and non-state actors via fake news, paid commentators, and propaganda bots; described by scholars like Tim Wu as a form of information control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft censorship / indirect influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Influencing news coverage indirectly, e.g., via financial pressure or rewards rather than overt legal bans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments or powerful actors may withhold funds or grant subsidies, fostering friendly coverage and punishing critical outlets; termed 'soft censorship' or 'media manipulation'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial censorship / debanking
rubrics_metrics.description: When financial institutions or payment intermediaries block, freeze, or inhibit transactions to limit what speech or content can exist online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include payment processing blocks against WikiLeaks; can take the form of deplatforming from financial services as pressure on speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common methods of censorship (mechanical and procedural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques used to suppress or alter information including blacklisting, bleeping, book burning, broadcast delay, prior restraint, redaction, pixelization, and content filtering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are applied across media and contexts; selection of methods depends on medium, legal regime, and objectives (e.g., removing specific content vs. broader suppression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet censorship methods and infrastructure control
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical and administrative methods for online censorship such as site blocking, content filtering, DNS control/seizure, takedowns, and national intranets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors leverage control of DNS, ISPs, app stores, search engines, and platform moderation tools; example: China's Golden Shield, domain seizures coordinated with law enforcement or ICANN actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated social media censorship and content removal patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of automated systems to delete or restrict social media posts, with deletion patterns influenced by content features (e.g., mentions of collective action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies (e.g., Gary King et al.) found posts mentioning collective action are more likely to be censored; automated moderation can be targeted to limit organizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional rating standards and content modification (video games, films)
rubrics_metrics.description: Content is edited or removed to comply with regional rating systems or legal standards (e.g., removing gore, sexual content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: No More Heroes had gore removed in Japanese/PAL versions; ESRB and other rating bodies drive edits to meet market/regulatory thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Film censorship and party-political definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws defining and restricting political films (e.g., Singapore's Films Act) and standards for allowable party political content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions ban 'party political films' or require factual/objective review; exceptions may be made for films supportive of ruling parties or about foreign politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveillance and the chilling effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveillance—whether or not followed by direct censorship—can produce a 'chilling effect' leading to self-censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widespread knowledge of monitoring (state or corporate) reduces willingness to speak freely; surveillance thus functions as a censorship mechanism even without overt takedown actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartographic (map) censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission, graying, or alteration of map data for military or security reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical uses include East Germany near border regions; modern examples include selective omission or outdated imagery on mapping services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Banning or restricting artworks deemed politically or morally unacceptable, often used for propaganda or moral enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Nazi 'degenerate art' bans, state control of artistic performances, and legal/political restrictions that can criminalize unsanctioned art or performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photography censorship and sanitization
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering or destroying photographs to remove undesired persons or content (sanitization of imagery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: Soviet altering of photos to remove purged individuals; modern instances include covers being stickered or edited for local markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal restrictions and jurisdiction-specific statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws and statutes that define forbidden speech or content and prescribe penalties (examples: India IT Rules 2011, Turkish Penal Code Art. 299, FCC v. Pacifica, R v. Butler).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions of 'objectionable' vary by jurisdiction (e.g., threats to unity, security, public order); enforcement includes fines, imprisonment, investigations, and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility of censorship and circumvention dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship's effectiveness depends on technical and institutional control; the distributed nature of the Internet makes total censorship difficult except under near-total control (e.g., North Korea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumvention tools (VPNs, alternative DNS roots, Freenet) and technical ingenuity often limit censorship, but resourceful, well-funded regimes can maintain extensive controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform practices: shadowbanning and localized moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Platform-specific moderation practices such as shadowbanning, hashtag categorization, and localization of guidelines that can effectively reduce visibility of certain content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: TikTok's tagging/limiting of certain hashtags; platform localization can produce varying censorship outcomes across countries and topics.
